Friday, November 6, 2026

All day La Mirada Boricua | Symposium | Day 1 Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

Image - Miguel Luciano, Vulture Brand Yams (2017).

Join us for Day 1 of La Mirada Boricua Symposium - View the Full Program Here.

La Mirada Boricua” translates as “The Boricua Gaze,” with “Boricua” derived from the Taíno indigenous name for Puerto Ricans. La Mirada Boricua is a faculty exhibition curated by Professor Israel Reyes of the Department of Spanish and Portuguese and hosted by the Hood Museum that explores contemporary Puerto Rican art and the intimate and public spaces it creates for engaging with the archipelago’s colonial history, the experience of migration and diaspora, and the possibilities for a decolonial future. 

La Mirada Boricua events are sponsored by The Department of Spanish & Portuguese, The Leslie Center for the Humanities, and the Hood Museum of Art.

12 pm - 1 pm From Slides to Solutions: Designing Course Materials for Every Student audience: Faculty, Postdoc, Staff, Students-Graduate DCAL Baker 102

Every student’s brain is wired differently, shaping how they understand and engage with the content you teach. As instructors, you have the power to create and present materials that facilitate deep engagement and learning. This hands-on session invites you to explore digital accessibility not as a compliance checklist, but as an act of intentional, inclusive teaching. Together we'll examine how accessibility barriers show up in slide decks or lecture materials and experiment with simple, practical changes that can transform the learning experience for your students. You'll leave with concrete skills and a fresh perspective on what it means to design for every learner in the room. Participants are asked to bring slides or lecture materials to develop into a slide deck during the session.

Register for From Slides to Solutions.

2:15 pm - 3:15 pm Physics and Astronomy Colloquium - Dr. Félix Beaudoin, Nanoacademic Technologies academic Wilder 104 and Zoom

Abstract: 

Scaling up quantum computers requires engineering quantum devices whose behavior is predictable, reproducible, and robust against imperfections. However, quantum hardware such as superconducting qubits or spin qubits in semiconductors suffer from atomic-scale defects and imperfections leading to decoherence and device-to-device variability, posing major challenges to scalability. In this colloquium, I will discuss how multiscale modeling bridges the gap between atomic-scale physics and device-scale physics, turning fundamental physics into a powerful quantum engineering tool. I will explain how, mirroring decades of engineering practice in the semiconductor industry, we are building multiscale simulation software that is increasingly used in the quantum industry to reduce trial-and-error and accelerate the development of fault-tolerant quantum computers. I will illustrate these ideas through recent work at Nanoacademic Technologies on two major quantum computing platforms. First, I will show how multiscale simulations can quantitatively reproduce the behavior of semiconductor spin qubits, including gate-defined and donor-based quantum dots. I will then discuss our recent efforts to model Josephson junctions, where atomic-scale defects and interface roughness can influence quantum transport and lead to device-to-device variability, whose impact is then captured in computational microwave engineering simulations combined with Hamiltonian analysis. These examples enable us to foresee a future in which materials and devices are engineered together, toward a quantum computer co-design paradigm grounded in fundamental solid-state physics.

Hosted by Professor Lorenza Viola

Zoom Webinar Link: https://dartmouth.zoom.us/j/91888702369?pwd=aUlaVEFYNGZHNlZWL0R3cEVWQXg4UT09

3:30 pm - 4:30 pm Combinatorial Synthesis of Ionic Materials Using Atomic Layer Deposition Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 937 4316 0035
Passcode: 411385

Solid state batteries (SSBs) are considered the most promising next-generation energy storage technology both due to their increased safety over conventional wet Li-ion cells and their ability to fabricate novel architectures with simultaneous high energy and power density. However, the ionic conductivities of many solid electrolyte materials are orders of magnitude lower than liquid carbonate-based electrolytes. In order to offer SSBs with competitive charge/discharge rates, SSB active layers need to be thin (for fast ion diffusion) but have a large surface area (to enable large ion flux from anode to cathode). These geometric constraints establish the need for 3D nanostructures for a high-performance battery architecture. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is ideally suited to fabricate such devices due to its highly conformal nature and Angstrom-scale thickness control, however many challenges remain with materials fabrication and process integration.

I will discuss development and progress in fabrication of both plasma-enhanced ALD (PEALD) and thermal ALD processes for the Li, Na, and K alkali polyphosphazene (A*PON) electrolytes. I will discuss and compare the reaction mechanisms and growth behavior among the entire family of A*PON solid electrolyte thin films, as well as discuss current progress and the integration challenges on the path to developing all-ALD planar and 3D SSBs. Lastly, I will discuss how high-throughput combinatorial strategies can facilitate synthesis of next-generation thin-film solid electrolyte materials.

Nov 6 Nov 13
6:00pm Songs of Old New Hampshire Waterville Valley Recreation Department Multi-Purpose Room 11 Noon Peak Rd Waterville Valley NH 03215

Drawing heavily on the repertoire of traditional singer Lena Bourne Fish (1873-1945) of Jaffrey and Temple, NH, Jeff Warner offers the songs and stories that, in the words of Carl Sandburg, tell us "where we came from and what brought us along." These ballads, love songs and comic pieces, reveal the experiences and emotions of daily life in the days before movies, sound recordings and, for some, books. Songs from the lumber camps, the decks of sailing ships, the textile mills, and the war between the sexes offer views of pre-industrial New England and a chance to hear living artifacts from the 18th and 19th centuries. 

Humanities to GoJeff WarnerThe Rey Cultural CenterLeah Elliot, leah@thereycenter.org

 ONE EVENT. TWO NONPROFITS. ONE AMAZING COMMUNITY!

Join Us for the Second Annual Artisan Soup Fundraiser!

Friday, November 6, 2026 | 6:00–8:00 PM
Enfield Shaker Museum | Great Stone Dwelling

Come warm your heart and fill your bowl at the Second Annual Artisan Soup Fundraiser! Join us for a delicious evening of homemade soups, fresh salads, and tempting desserts while supporting two wonderful local nonprofits: Enfield Shaker Museum and Jezzie’s Place!

 A Handmade Bowl with Every Ticket!

Every ticket purchased includes your choice of a beautiful handmade bowl or mug generously donated by local potters. Take home a unique piece of local artistry while enjoying a wonderful meal and supporting two meaningful causes.

 Meet Jezzie’s Place

Jezzie’s Place is a local, ethical dog rescue based in Canaan, New Hampshire. Founded in 2024 by Haley and her husband, this organization is dedicated to helping pets and animals throughout the Upper Valley.

Their mission is to provide care, compassion, and support to animals in need. We are excited to bring our community together to support their important work alongside the preservation, education, and community programs of Enfield Shaker Museum.

 Help Us Support Jezzie’s Place!

There are many ways to make a difference! In addition to joining us for the fundraiser, please consider donating supplies or making a monetary contribution to help Jezzie’s Place continue caring for local animals.http://www.jezziesplace.com

 Jezzie’s Place Wish List

  • Peanut butter — must be xylitol-free!
  • Applesauce
  • Pill pockets — peanut butter flavor is a favorite!
  • Crunchy O’s treats
  • Black KONG toys
  • Nature’s Miracle cleaning products
  • Hefty Ultra Strong 30-gallon trash bags
  • Laundry Boost products

 Prefer to make a monetary donation?

You can also support Jezzie’s Place with a donation of:

  • $20
  • $60

Every donation, big or small, helps provide essential supplies and care for animals in need. Your generosity truly makes a difference!

 One Evening. Two Meaningful Causes.

Enjoy a delicious meal, choose a handmade treasure, and help make a positive impact in our community.

Whether you’re joining us for the soup, supporting local artists, helping preserve our shared history, or lending a hand to animals in need, your participation matters.

Gather your friends, bring your appetite, and join us for an evening filled with wonderful food, local artistry, and community spirit!

 Come for the soup. Leave knowing you’ve made a difference!

COCKTAIL RECEPTION & ART EXHIBIT

During the evening, artists Tim Jennings and Tami DeFelice will have their artwork on display for viewing and purchase.

Enjoy a cocktail, mingle with fellow guests, and take in the artwork in the beautiful historic setting of the Great Stone Dwelling.

Cash and credit cards accepted for cocktails and artwork purchases.

YOUR TICKET INCLUDES:

  • One handcrafted bowl or mug of your choosing
  • Unlimited artisan soups,
  • Fresh salads

7 pm - 9 pm Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

The 2026 Cannes Queer Palm winner, Jane Schoenbrun's love letter to slashers starring Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder revels in desire, discovery and bloodshed.

After years of slapdash sequels and waning fandom, the Camp Miasma slasher franchise is handed over to an enthusiastic young director (Hannah Einbinder) for resurrection. But when she visits the original's star (Gillian Anderson), a now-reclusive actress shrouded in mystery, the two women fall into a blood-soaked world of desire, fear and delirium. 

Director Jane Schoenbrun (I Saw the TV Glow) knows every rule of the genre—and gleefully breaks them. In addition to Schoenbrun behind the camera, the film features memorable supporting turns from trans artists like Louise Weard (Castration Movie) and Avalon Fast (Camp).

Programmed in collaboration with the Office of Pluralism and Leadership for Trans Visibility Week

 

Get more info and tickets here.

9:00 am Twill Bread Tray Workshop Enfield Shaker Museum

$50 – $60

Versatile Tote Basket

With Dona Nazarenko

November 7, 2026 

9:00 am – 5:00 pm

Whether you are looking to add a homemade touch your table, to make a gift for the holiday season, or even to learn a new skill, then this decorative yet functional twill bread tray workshop is for you! Join us at the Enfield Shaker Museum and basket maker Dona Nazarenko on November 7th for an all day workshop. The class will be using dyed and natural reed, with color choices available to make each basket uniquely yours. The final basket will be about 9″ x 15″ x 2 1/2″ high.

Who is Doña Nazerenko?

Residing in Tunbridge, Vermont, Doña Nazarenko has been weaving since 1988 and teaching since 1994. While living along the New Jersey coast, Doña developed an interest in woodcrafts and related art forms that developed into her desire to take basket making classes in 1988.

Her exploration of a different art medium has since evolved into a flourishing talent. She now enjoys making traditional baskets using reed with wooden accents to more challenging baskets using birch bark from the area surrounding her current residence in rural Vermont.

The highlight of the early years at her craft was having a one-on-one critique with John McGuire at Peter’s Gallery in 1992. His confidence in her and his discretion continues to help her with her current work. Today she can be seen demonstrating basketry representing Vermont fiber artists at local and out-of-state events. Most days she can be found working in her studio at Country Spirit Baskets

Please bring your own lunch. Water and light refreshments will be provided.

Cost:

Museum Members – $50

Non-Members – $60

All proceeds go to the educational mission of Enfield Shaker Museum.

4 pm - 7 pm The Neighbors – Closing Reception 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center

Closing Reception 
Nov 7, 2026 4PM - 7PM

Join Associate Professor of Studio Art Chris Sollars for snacks in the 0102 gallery, Visual Arts Center. His faculty exhibition, The Neighbors, is on view Sept. 15 – Nov. 8.

In his first solo exhibition at Dartmouth College, multidisciplinary artist and Associate Professor of Studio Art Chris Sollars presents The Neighbors, a new body of work inspired by coexistence and inquiry.
Set in rural Vermont, The Neighbors is a multimedia video installation about the non-human inhabitants of the lands around the artist’s home. After over two decades living in San Francisco, California, Sollars moved to Vermont in the fall of 2024. To get to know his new home and neighbors, he has spent the past two years interacting with his surroundings through slow listening and observation, learning them spatially and temporally.  This intentional gathering of information has taken the form of diaristic snapshots taken throughout the seasons, field recordings, the collection of discarded nests and materials, and the placement of wildlife cameras in the open woodland edges of his home, which neighbors a land trust, a national forest, and the Appalachian Trail.

Read the review of The Neighbors Exhibition in Seven Days by Alice Dodge.

4 pm - 6 pm The Return (DFS: Myths Revisited) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Ralph Fiennes plays Odysseus in Uberto Pasolini's grounded, realistic adaptation of Homer's dramatic final act.

Stripped of the familiar mythological monsters and gods, Odysseus (Ralph Fiennes) and Penelope (Juliette Binoche) reunite on an Ithaca devoid of the usual fantasy or epic. 
Sweeping visuals are traded for intimate closeups, and the raw, human emotion of Odysseus' return takes center stage rather than its marvel or grandeur. 

Using minimalism, natural light and the story's inherent moral and psychological conflicts, Pasolini crafts a powerful and unforgettable entry into The Odyssey catalog. Fiennes and Binoche carry the film with quiet intensity, making us feel as though we're actually watching the real Odysseus and Penelope reunite. For scholars and cinephiles alike, this is not an adaptation to be missed.

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited"

10 am - 11 am PhD Thesis Defense: Emma Graham academic Rm 232, Cummings Hall (Jackson Conf Rm)/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Many problems and observations of the world can be represented as sequences. Sequence modeling bears on how we solve problems and represent information, and on how small, ordered components give rise to properties that none of them has alone. Deep sequence models now write fluent text and predict protein structures, and are increasingly integrated into consequential settings. Yet apparent competence does not by itself establish what a model can compute. 

Two questions guide this dissertation: Does a model have the computational ability for your task? Under what conditions do its computations remain reliable? Drawing on the theory of computation, it studies computations of sequences from five directions: sequences generated by grammars of known computational classes, benchmarks of pretrained language models on those sequences, the design of a new deep sequence model, an analysis of its computations, and its implementation on a sequence task.

Asked a simple question, is this sentence grammatical?, frontier AI models disagree with people and with one another. On generated sentences whose dependencies exceed those of any known natural-language rule, human participants and nearly all conventional large language models answered no. Models with added inference-time computation effort answered yes far more often, and more so as that effort increased.

These evaluations motivate a new model architecture, the Lattice-Induction State-Space Sequence Model (LiSSM), which combines continuous state with learned logical relations. LiSSM can simulate a universal counter machine, which makes it Turing-complete under exact-arithmetic, unbounded-state, and unbounded-time assumptions. A separate result proves that any prescribed finite execution of this simulation keeps its decoded symbolic states under perturbation, provided accumulated error stays within an explicit margin. Built into a Logical Recurrent Network block, LiSSM matched or exceeded Mamba and transformer baselines on an initial selective-copying task.

Together, these results build toward a fundamental understanding of sequence models, one that accounts for what a model does, what its architecture can represent, and which of its computations are reliable. The more these models are trusted in high-stakes settings, the more we need to know their abilities and limits, and the assumptions under which they hold.

Thesis Committee: Richard Granger (chair), George Cybenko, Bryce Ferguson, Brooks Paige (University College London)

7:00pm Henry Dearborn - From Captain to Cabinet Secretary Morgera Mtg. Room Stratham Fire Station 4 Winnicutt Rd. Stratham NH 03885

In this presentation, George Morrison explores the life and career of Henry Dearborn, born in North Hampton, New Hampshire in 1751. He began his career as a young doctor before joining the the Contintental Army, where he served for over eight years. Post-war he served two terms in Congress, later as a cabinet secretary, and was, before retiring in 1824, President Monroe’s Minister to Portugal. But in 1818 he found himself in the middle of a controversy that would extend to 1843. Would you rather be elected governor, or insist on telling the truth? 

Meeting room is on the ground floor and handicap accessible from the large, free parking lot.

7:00pm The Ethics of AI Virtual Southern New Hampshire University 2500 North River Road Manchester NH 03106

This program explores some of the most urgent moral challenges that Artificial Intelligence presents to society today. Topics include automation and job displacement, deepfakes and misinformation, the role of AI in education, implicit bias, autonomous systems (such as self-driving cars and drones), and the ethical implications of a potential technological singularity. After a brief introduction to applied ethics and the technology behind generative AI, we will examine each issue in turn, highlighting the core moral questions they raise and their significance for shaping sound policies and regulations. The session will conclude with an open discussion, giving attendees a chance to share perspectives and ask questions. Participants will come away with a clearer understanding of the ethical landscape of AI and the tools to think critically about its future impact.

12 pm - 1 pm DCC Grand Rounds with Goutham Narla, MD, PhD DHMC, Auditorium E

Dr. Goutham Narla is a physician scientist and trained as a medical geneticist in the care of high-risk cancer and medical genetics patients.  Clinically, Dr. Narla leads the Division of Genetic Medicine that cares for over 3000 high-risk cancer and medical genetics patients per year. His research interests are in the study of the mechanisms that regulate oncogene and tumor suppressor function in human cancer. Specifically, his research focuses on understanding the mechanisms driving human cancer development and progression and has led to: 1) the identification of a new class of tumor suppressor genes in human cancer, 2) the characterization of novel mechanisms of tumor suppressor gene inactivation in cancer progression,  3) the development and validation of pharmaceutically tractable strategies to reactive tumor suppressor gene function for the treatment of a broad range of human cancers, and 4) the structural, functional and biological mechanisms of PP2A inactivation in human cancer. This work has been published in some of the top scientific journals. These novel small-molecule tumor suppressor gene activators represent the first, to our knowledge, example of drugs that directly bind and activate tumor suppressor genes for cancer treatment and provide the mechanistic and translational framework/foundation to develop entire classes of drugs directed at the key negative regulators of oncogenic signaling, an area that to date has not been the focus of major drug development efforts. Based upon these discoveries he co-founded a biotechnology company, RAPPTA Therapeutics, which has obtained a significant amount of funding to fund the preclinical development of these first-in-class series of PP2A molecular glues (PMGs) from an investment syndicate led by Novartis Ventures, Novo Holdings and Advent Life Sciences.

Join the Department of Film & Media Studies for our fall colloquium with Technical Director, Warren Cockerham.

Warren Cockerham is a filmmaker, educater, and cinema technologist. He recevied his MFA from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 2010. His early work in media access and advocacy led to the founding of FilmLAB@1512, a film and video program for teenagers in Chicago's North Lawndale community.

His film work is driven by an interest in power structures within familial and intimate relationships, and how those dynamics are shaped, obscured, or reframed through archival media–both public and private. His projects tend to resist conventional narrative, instead organizing themselves around a set of problems or tensions. His work has screened at venues across the U.S. and internationally.

2 pm - 3 pm PhD Thesis Defense: Vincent Chen academic Rm 101, MacLean ESC/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Fair healthcare decision-making seeks outcomes close to those achieved by an oracle policy that maximizes expected benefit without fairness constraints. It also aims to reduce unjustified variation in decisions and outcomes. Existing optimization and machine learning approaches often lack explicit mechanisms to promote comparable decisions for patients with similar clinical needs. This dissertation examines fairness across healthcare decision-making, from conceptual frameworks to treatment planning and patient routing.

First, a systematic review examines fairness in healthcare optimization and machine learning. It screens 801 references and identifies 114 relevant studies, categorizing sources of bias, fairness metrics, and mitigation strategies. The findings establish a foundation for choosing fairness criteria according to clinical and operational contexts.

Second, we develop fair distributional reinforcement learning for individualized hypertension treatment planning. The algorithm models distributions of long-term outcomes and applies Cram.r-distance regularization to patients with comparable clinical characteristics. An additional post-update correction uses constrained interpolation or fallback mixing to move estimated return distributions toward high performing subgroup references. Independent simulations evaluate learned policies using quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). Compared with standard distributional reinforcement learning, QALYs for representative vulnerable patients increase from 29.75 to 31.32 in the low-risk group. Corresponding increases are from 24.46 to 25.86 and from 17.06 to 18.69 in intermediate- and high-risk groups, respectively.

Third, we develop a fairness-aware contextual bandit for assigning triage priorities in a medical guidance application. The application recommends appropriate care levels. The framework selects low, medium, or high priority while balancing clinical need, resource use, and local fairness constraints. Its policy adapts patient representations and subgroup estimates using feedback, and the selected priority guides response generation. Across 83,604 held-out emergency-department visits, priority conditioning improves evaluated response quality by 8.9% to 9.7% across three model families. The largest improvement is 15.1% among medium-priority patients.

Together, these studies show how clinical comparability can inform fairness criteria, improve simulated treatment outcomes, and guide urgency-sensitive patient communication. They connect fairness in healthcare to both downstream treatment planning and upstream patient routing.

Thesis Committee: Wesley Marrero (chair), Eugene Santos Jr, Peter Chin, Shuhang Wang (Walmart Global Tech)

4:30 pm - 6:00 pm Honoring All Who Served: Veterans Day Observance Haldeman 041 and Online

“As we honor those that have worn the uniform of our armed forces, Veteran's Day provides an opportunity to reflect on how their leadership and character forged in the crucible of military service continue to serve our nation.” 

Lieutenant General John Broadmeadow retired from the Marine Corps in October 2020 as a three-star general with nearly forty years of progressive leadership experience in a variety of positions. He successfully led large, diverse organizations across the globe, in combat and during periods of significant change. After retiring from the Marine Corps he leveraged extensive experience in executive leadership, strategic planning, and corporate change management by consulting in the private sector and with various government organizations.

Broadmeadow’s final Marine Corps assignment was as the Director of the Marine Corps Staff in the Pentagon. In addition to leading Headquarters Marine Corps’ response to COVID-19, he integrated the actions of seven three-star Deputy Commandants executing a Marine Corps-wide change management effort to implement the Commandant’s Planning Guidance.

In his first three-star job he was assigned as the Deputy Commander of the United States Transportation Command, proudly serving with the more than 140,000 service members and civilians from across all the Armed Services providing globally integrated air, sea, and surface transportation for all personnel and cargo in the U.S. Department of Defense.

Broadmeadow’s career includes several notable accomplishments in expeditionary operations. He led the logistics planning and execution for the Marines’ initial amphibious assault into Afghanistan in 2001 immediately following the attacks of 9/11. He then served multiple tours in both Iraq and Afghanistan, including as the lead advisor to the 7th Iraqi Infantry Division in 2009 and culminating with leading the drawdown and retrograde of equipment from Helmand Province in 2013. He’s also experienced with Humanitarian Operations, having led forces in both Somalia for Operation Restore Hope and in Japan following the earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear plant damage that devastated the coast north of Tokyo. As a General Officer, he commanded a Marine Expeditionary Brigade and both the Marine Corps Logistics Command and Marine Corps Installations Command, each having multi-billion-dollar portfolios.

After his Marine Corps retirement, Broadmeadow was asked to sit as a Panel Member for the Department of the Navy’s Strategic Review of Amphibious Operations and as an Executive Fellow for the Institute for Defense and Business. He is an Advisory Board Member for Crowley, a Senior Mentor for the Marine Corps’ MAGTF Staff Training Program, and a member of the Marine Corps Association Board of Directors.

Broadmeadow is the highest-ranking Marine Officer to have graduated from Norwich and is honored to have received the Distinguished Alumni Award and have his name engraved on the Bicentennial Stairs. He has served on the Norwich University Board of Trustees since February 2022. 

Free and open to the public, tickets required, get yours here.  Recorded and livestreamed, register for the webinar here. 

In collaboration with the Davidson Institute for Global Security at Dartmouth and the Nelson A. Rockefeller Center for Public Policy at Dartmouth.

6 pm - 8 pm Vets Town Hall Georgiopoulos Classroom, Raether Hall

At a Vets Town Hall event, veterans of any era who served in any capacity have the right to stand before their community and speak for up to ten minutes about what it was like to serve their country.

Some speakers may be proud, others may be angry and a few may be crying too hard to speak. But those feelings should processed by the entire nation, rather than just by veterans themselves. Vets Town Hall events are a way to start making that happen.

This is not a political event. War is an inherently divisive topic, but the important conversation around how and when our nation goes to war has no place in a Vets Town Hall.

There are no “activists” or “patriots” at these events; no “liberals” or “conservatives.” There are just veterans who are willing to speak openly about their experiences, and community members who are willing to listen.

Do not underestimate the incredible power of that process.

7:00pm Lafayette’s Farewell Tour: The Granite State Salutes the Nation’s Guest Meredith Community Center 1 Circle Drive Meredith NH 03253

On his fourth and final trip to the United States in 1824-1825, Americans in all 24 states welcomed Lafayette with unbridled admiration, gratitude, and love. In this talk, Hoffman will set the scene for the Farewell Tour and explore the causes of Lafayette’s rock star reception. 

Then, he will turn to Lafayette’s visits to New Hampshire cities and towns and describe how the Granite Staters added their voices to this national outpouring of affection. Visits to Portsmouth on September 1, 1824, and Concord on June 22, 1825, will be featured, as they were highlights of the General’s New Hampshire experience. Hoffman will also describe Lafayette’s stops in the other New Hampshire towns that Lafayette visited on the Tour. 

Doors open at 6:30; light refreshments served.

3:30 pm - 4:15 pm Guided Relaxation with iRest yoga Nidra, and Journaling Rollins Chapel

The SWC is excited to bring you a mid-week restorative practice* with to-go healthy snacks and journals!

This experiential learning opportunity will take place every Wednesday from 3:30 to 4:15pm. Each session will look something like this: 
- Setup mats and settle into our spaces (5- minutes) 
- Guided yoga nidra (25- minutes)
- Prompted free-write in provided journals (6 minutes)
- Debrief and optional sharing time (6 min) 
- Ending session and putting away mats, journals (3 minutes) 

*mats will be provided

What is Yoga Nidra?

Yoga nidra is a type of meditation practice originating from ancient India, commonly known as "yogic sleep" or "dynamic sleep." It is a contemplative practice that involves following guided prompts while lying in a comfortable position through various stages of relaxation, breathing exercises, and visualization.

This practice aims to induce a state of deep relaxation and meditation, similar to the liminal state between waking and sleeping. This state can provide numerous physical, emotional, and mental benefits, such as reducing stress and anxiety, improving sleep, enhancing creativity, and promoting overall well-being. In this state, you may experience a sense of timelessness, expansiveness, and interconnectedness.

9 am - 10 am PhD Thesis Defense: Peter Bertone academic Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Reconstruction of bone defects after cancer resection is complicated by radiotherapy (RTx), which impairs bone healing and limits bone grafting effectivity. Engineered bone graft substitutes offer an alternative but have been developed almost exclusively in non-irradiated conditions. This dissertation examines how therapeutic RTx affects a biomaterial based bone-graft substitute (Chitosan-Gelatin cryogel scaffold), and the healing environment into which this material is implanted.

This work first establishes a composite scaffold combining the cryogel with a 3D-printed, sintered bio-ceramic structure to improve its physical properties and bioactivity (hydroxyapatite–wollastonite lattice). Then, to further understand RTx interaction with the polymer gel, this work characterizes the physical, chemical, and biological stability of the cryogel across a clinically relevant single-fraction dose range. Finally, this work evaluates bone healing in a mouse femoral critical defect model under single-fraction and fractionated RTx, with and without an implanted scaffold. Together, these studies probe the combined healing environment of biopolymer implants in bone after radiation treatment. 

Thesis Committee: Katherine Hixon (Chair), Douglas Van Citters, Joseph Paydarfar, Joel Boerckel (UPenn)

12 pm - 1 pm Biomedical Data Science Seminar academic DHMC, Auditorium H (and via Zoom)

Presenter: José R. Zubizarreta, PhD, Daniel C. Tosteson Professor of Health Care Policy at Harvard Medical School & Professor of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

The presentation will take place both in person at DHMC, Auditorium H (and via Zoom) and we encourage as many of you to attend in person as possible.

Light refreshments will be provided on a first-come, first-served basis.

Please write to biomedical.data.science@dartmouth.edu to request the Zoom login details.

Please see description below for more details.

Please invite your fellow faculty colleagues, research associates, graduate trainees, and post-docs!

 

Presentation Summary
In observational studies, a fitted model may yield an estimate of a treatment effect without making explicit the comparison on which that estimate rests. Which observations are compared, and how much does each contribute? Which features of a randomized experiment, if any, does the comparison reproduce? These questions arise in spatial regressions with Gaussian process errors, two-way fixed effects analyses of staggered policy adoption, and mixed effects meta-analyses of trials. In this lecture, we derive exact, closed-form weighting representations of these estimators. In each case, the weights solve a common optimization problem that minimizes their dispersion subject to balance requirements. These finite-sample identities make explicit the comparisons implicit in the models, providing a basis for examining their causal interpretation and reconsidering their model specification. (i) For spatial data, specifying the error structure of a linear model is equivalent to including a set of hidden covariates under a particular form of regularization. (ii) For panel data, the weights reveal how two-way fixed effects and related estimators borrow information across units and time periods, clarifying the assumptions about the dynamics of treatment effects needed to justify that borrowing. (iii) For meta-analytic data, the weights identify studies and observations that are poorly aligned with the covariate distribution of the target population, helping to assess when their exclusion is prudent. These representations give rise to diagnostics that open the analysis to scrutiny, and they bring methods that appear unrelated onto common ground.
 
 
Biography  
José R. Zubizarreta, PhD, is the Daniel C. Tosteson Professor of Health Care Policy at Harvard Medical School, Professor of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, and a Faculty Affiliate in the Department of Statistics at Harvard University. His research focuses on developing statistical methods for causal inference to advance health care and public policy. Dr. Zubizarreta earned his PhD in Statistics from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, an MA in Economics from Universidad de Chile, and an undergraduate degree in Engineering from Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. A former Fulbright Scholar, Dr. Zubizarreta has received research support from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Warren Alpert Foundation, and other major research organizations. He serves as an Associate Editor for several leading journals, including the Annals of Applied Statistics, the Harvard Data Science Review, and the Journal of the American Statistical Association. Dr. Zubizarreta is an elected Fellow of the American Statistical Association (ASA). His honors include the Kenneth Rothman, William Cochran, and Tom Ten Have Memorial Awards, as well as the ASA’s Mid-Career Excellence Award in Health Policy Statistics. Dr. Zubizarreta has also received the Myrto Lefkopoulou Distinguished Lectureship at Harvard.

12:15 pm - 1:15 pm Teaching Writing with Integrity with Dr. Lily Abadal audience: Faculty, Postdoc, Staff, Students-Graduate DCAL (Baker 102)

If you have ever assigned any form of prose in your classes, you know that AI has completely upended the norms of assessment. Most instructors have responded with one of three approaches. Some have opted to employ AI detection software to sniff out phony student work. Others have replaced take-home essays with blue book exams where students demonstrate their knowledge in short form in less than two hours. Finally, others have ditched the essay entirely and have instead opted for oral exams and video reflection assignments.

This talk suggests there is another, better way to keep the formative benefits of the essay without the worry that students will over-rely on AI: a scaffolded, in-class, term-long paper. We will cover how to scaffold in-class argumentative writing with a view toward cultivating the patience, humility, and honesty that genuine inquiry requires.

Lunch will be provided. Please register!

Dr. Lily Abadal is an Assistant Professor of Instruction in the Judy Genshaft Honors College at the University of South Florida. She specializes in normative ethics, applied ethics, moral psychology, and philosophy of education. Her research and work sit at the intersection of AI ethics and character formation and she explore all things through a Neo-Aristotelian lens. Dr. Abadal applies her research and experience on human formation as a consultant at Partners in Mission, helping schools discern how to prudently integrate AI technology (in both operations and in the classroom) without diminishing the goods that make life worth living.

Tess Martin is an award-winning filmmaker/visual artist based in Rotterdam, The Netherlands. Many of her projects exist simultaneously as films and installations, often incorporating sculptural elements and individually experienced soundtracks to create intimate durational encounters. She often works with tactile materials such as paper cutouts, paint, ink, sand, and found objects, pushing the boundaries between animation and contemporary art.

1 pm - 2 pm Psychological and Brain Sciences Colloquium academic · audience: Alumni, Faculty, Postdoc, Staff, Students-Graduate, Students-Undergraduate Filene Auditorium, Moore Building

All dates: Nov 12, Nov 19

Please join us for a colloquium in Moore Filene Auditorium on Thursday, November 12, 2026, beginning at 1:10 p.m.

The talk will be presented by Anthony D. Wagner, Lucie Stern Professor in the Department of Psychology and Deputy Director of the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute at Stanford University.

Title:  Remembering Events Past: Multi-System Interactions for Building and Retrieving Memories

Abstract:  Episodic memory bridges the past and present, guides perception, thinking, and action in the moment, and supports simulation of possible futures. Successful building of event memories and their subsequent reactivation depend on interactions among multiple neurocognitive systems. In this talk, I will discuss medial temporal lobe, visual cortical, and top-down modulatory mechanisms of memory. First, I will set the stage by providing evidence for computational differentiation within the medial temporal lobe (MTL), wherein MTL cortical and hippocampal learning mechanisms support the encoding of event features and the conjunctions of features, respectively, and thus support distinct forms of subsequent memory. I will then turn to factors that influence how precisely visual cortex represents the features of events. I will draw on work in older adults, whose feature representations are often less precise, showing that the precision of event feature representation depends on multiple mechanisms, including top-down attention and local processes. Finally, I will discuss how preparatory attention modulates the representation of mnemonic goals, and in turn impacts the probability of memory retrieval. Collectively, these findings illustrate the complex neurocognitive symphony that underlies learning from events and empowers future remembering and memory-guided behavior.

Coffee, tea, and cider donuts will be available shortly before and after the talk.

11:30 am - 1:30 pm Physics and Astronomy PhD Defense - Brent Harrison, Dartmouth Haldeman 041 and Zoom

Abstract: In order to simulate a system of fermions on a quantum computer, it is first necessary to represent the system via a suitable fermion-to-qubit encoding. We investigate the space of all such encodings, and construct a unifying graph- and group-theoretic framework for them, over which one may optimize for target Hamiltonians and hardware connectivity constraints. We show that an important class of fermion-to-qubit encodings is dual to a class of classical data structures. Via this duality, we prove new cell-probe bounds in the classical setting, and synthesize new, optimal data-structure based encodings in the quantum setting. As an application of fermion-to-qubit encodings, we find a mapping between circle graph states and fermionic gaussian states, and hence resolve an open question regarding universal resources for Measurement-Based Quantum Computing. 

Graduate Student Advisor: Professor James Whitfield

3:30 pm - 4:30 pm Aeroplastic Design for Space Structures Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 937 4316 0035
Passcode: 411385

Turbine disks that are used in oxygen-rich turbopumps for reusable rocket engines are subjected to centrifugal forces from high-speed rotation and rapid cyclic thermal transients. These loading conditions are challenging to mitigate in order to maximize thermal performance for engine efficiency while avoiding burst, fatigue, and frictional ignition failures. Typically, yield-limited design rules are used to avoid thermal fatigue failures while still maximizing allowable thermal gradients in the disk.

In this study, alternative design rules are considered that leverage the plastic reserve while still safeguarding against burst and frictional ignition. In particular, both finite life design strategies and design rules based on the underused elastoplastic shakedown phenomenon are explored.

Sanford Diehl, NYU
Talk Title: "Respect, Directed Obligation, and Recognition"
Abstract: "What is it to respect another person? According to an influential view, it is to treat them as a bearer of rights to whom you have correlative duties. I will argue that this view cannot make sense of respect and disrespect through emotions and other nonvoluntary attitudes, and does not reflect that part of what we respect in other people is another evaluative point of view on the world, including on oneself. Instead I will suggest that respect for other people is a species of recognition, by which I mean a way of taking someone to count that they can see themselves in and inhabit in relation to you."

10:00 am Make A Turkey Wing Whisk Broom Enfield Shaker Museum

$65 – $75

Turkey Wing Whisk Broom Workshop

Saturday, November 14, 2026

10:00 am – 4:00 pm

During the 19th century, the Enfield Shakers produced as many as “2000 dozen” brooms per year. Begun at Watervliet, New York community, in 1798, the Shaker broom industry quickly became one of the most important industries for Shaker communities across the country. Brooms can also be seen as a symbol of an important Shaker ideal. Cleanliness was a spiritual and moral imperative. When Mother Ann Lee told her followers, “Sweep clean,” she was referring not only to the floor of the home, but also the floor of the heart.

Join our resident broom squire Larry Antonuk for a Turkey Wing Whisk Broom Workshop. Begin by learning to make a simple bundle whisk broom, including the knots and materials used to make all brooms. After you master the skills necessary to use a “tumble spool”, you will move on to the more challenging turkey wing whisk broom. Students will end the class with multiple hand brooms and an understanding of many new techniques

These traditional, functional, high quality and long lasting brooms are made from natural broom corn.

This Turkey Wing Whisk Broom workshop takes place in the historic Great Stone Dwelling dining room. Participants will have the opportunity to explore the Brethren’s West Shop and the historical equipment the Shaker Brother’s used to create their iconic brooms.

Class size limited to 8. Advance registration required.

Please bring a bag lunch, closed-toe shoes and a water bottle.

Cost: 

Museum Members – $65/per person (includes materials)

Non-Members – $75/per person (includes materials)

*Please select the quantity of tickets you would like before clicking the “Get Tickets” button.

All proceeds from this workshop go to support the educational mission of Enfield Shaker Museum.

Coming from a distance? Why not plan to stay overnight in the historic Great Stone Dwelling? Check out room availability here.

More about our Broom Squire Larry Antonuk:

Sometime in 2010, Larry Antonuk found himself on a tour of the Enfield Shaker Museum. While watching a Broom Making demonstration he became fascinated with the process, and wound up coming back for a private tutorial with Master Broom Maker Susan Brown.

One thing led to another, and Larry is now a frequent demonstrator at the Museum. He has researched and reproduced a variety of Shaker designs, and now sells his work in our Gift Shop. Larry is a juried member of the League of NH Craftsmen, and can often be seen demonstrating at the Sunapee Fair.

4:00pm Redcoats & Rebels: New Hampshire and the American Revolution The Lakes Gallery 135 Eastman Road Laconia New Hampshire 03246

New Hampshire often gets overlooked in the narrative of the American Revolution, overshadowed by its noisy neighbor to the south. Nowadays, few people know about Paul Revere’s first ride, which was to Portsmouth in December 1774 to warn the patriots that the British were coming to reinforce Fort William and Mary, five months before the Redcoats marched on Concord and Lexington. Nor do they know that two-thirds of the troops at the Battle of Bunker Hill were from New Hampshire. Most people are also unaware that New Hampshire’s Provincial Congress adopted the first state constitution in January 1776, making no mention of royal authority and essentially declaring independence from Great Britain six months before anyone else. And this is just the beginning of New Hampshire’s revolutionary story. This program is presented as part of the New Hampshire Historical Society's celebration of America's 250th.

10 am - 11 am MS Thesis Defense: Ada Yildirim academic Rm 232, Cummings Hall (Jackson Conf Rm)/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Predictive control requires the controller to possess an embedded prediction model. In multi-agent control, this prediction model must consider the behavior that emerges from other agents' strategic decisions. Game theory offers a natural model for the emergent collective behavior of self-interested agents. Model predictive games (MPGs) are a class of controllers in which an agent iteratively solves a finite-horizon game to predict the behavior of a multi-agent system and synthesize their own control action. When all agents use the same game model to select their control action, conditions have been found that guarantee the stability of the multi-agent system. However, when multiple agents implement their own MPG controllers, their respective game models may be misspecified due to inaccurate estimates or conjectures about other agents' objectives, resulting in heterogeneous MPG controllers. This thesis analyzes the consequences of these prediction misalignments on the system's behavior. Using a two-agent example, we show that existing stability conditions for homogeneous MPG controllers do not extend to the heterogeneous setting, even when they hold for each agent's individual game. The closed-loop system is defined as the linear system dynamics in feedback with the agents' Nash equilibrium maps obtained from their heterogeneous MPG controllers, and analyzed with the tools of dissipativity and monotone operator theory. Sufficient conditions for the stability of multi-agent dynamical systems with heterogeneous MPG controllers adopting strongly monotone linear-quadratic game models are provided in a linear matrix inequality (LMI) form. The sensitivity of the closed-loop equilibrium to individual agents' game parameters is quantified via parametric variational inequality theory. In a financial duopoly simulation, the closed-loop stability is analyzed for increasing levels of misspecification and prediction horizons via the derived stability certificate. The results show that heterogeneous game models alone can destabilize a multi-agent system, and that the LMI offers a verifiable stability certificate.

Thesis Committee: Bryce L. Ferguson (Chair), Richard Granger, and Wesley Marrero

2 pm - 3 pm PhD Thesis Defense: Yieljae Shin academic Rm 005, ECSC/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Recording from large populations of neurons at cellular resolution is central to neuroscience and to brain–computer interfaces. Polymer-based thin-film electrode arrays are well suited to this goal, because they can be microfabricated at scale with cellular-size electrodes and are thin and flexible enough to approach the mechanics of neural tissue. Scaling these arrays from tens to thousands of channels, however, is not simply a matter of adding electrodes: each increase in channel count exposes a limit at a different level of the device. This thesis treats scaling as a multi-level problem and develops one strategy for each of four levels, volumetric, interconnect, electrochemical and mechanical, on a common platform.

At the volumetric level, planar fabrication confines electrodes to two dimensions. The rolling-of-soft-electronics (ROSE) approach converts a planar array of flexible shanks into a monolithic three-dimensional probe in a deterministic way, preserving its electrical performance and enabling high-yield volumetric recordings in rodents and a nonhuman primate. At the interconnect level, a passive array requires a dedicated trace and connector pad for every electrode, so the interconnect footprint grows with channel count. For NeuroCROWN, an actively multiplexed probe built on foundry complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) circuitry, this thesis developed the post-fabrication and transfer-printing process that turns a rigid chip into a flexible, implantable shank, which recorded depth-dependent auditory-evoked potentials in vivo. At the electrochemical level, coating many small electrodes uniformly becomes increasingly difficult. Potentiostatic electroplating of poly (3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) holds every electrode at the same potential and produces array-wide uniform, low-impedance coatings. At the mechanical level, shanks must be thin to limit tissue damage, but thinning a shank makes it harder to insert. Validated on single polyimide shanks, local sharpening and tungsten reinforcement of the tip roughly halved the force needed to puncture a brain phantom without stiffening the rest of the shank.

Together, these strategies show that the limits that arise at each level of scaling can be addressed with processes compatible with conventional microfabrication, providing a path toward very-large-scale, flexible three-dimensional neural interfaces.

Thesis Committee: Hui Fang (chair); William Scheideler; Alexander Boys; Jonathan Viventi (Duke University)

9 am - 10 am PhD Thesis Defense: Ngoc Minh Bui academic Rm B45, ECSC (Conference Room)/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract:

This dissertation is organized around three main research themes: geometric data structures for feature representation, adversarial analysis of privacy in federated speech systems, and computational efficiency in audio signal processing.

  1. **Enhancing GMRA for High-Dimensional Feature Extraction.** We present improvements to the Geometric Multi-Resolution Analysis (GMRA) framework for feature extraction from high-dimensional and non-Euclidean data, including images and graph-structured data. By refining multiscale geometric approximations, this work captures the intrinsic manifold structure of complex datasets and enables more robust representation learning than standard linear dimensionality reduction methods. We further introduce a dictionary learning approach to enhance the feature representation capabilities of GMRA.
  2. **Gradient Leakage Attacks on Federated Speech Recognition.** Building on prior studies of Differential Privacy (DP) vulnerabilities in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems, this research investigates the robustness of decentralized acoustic models. We address information leakage by extending zero-order optimization attack frameworks to first-order optimization methods, improving the efficiency and accuracy of private data reconstruction from model updates. We further extend this setting to token-based audio language models and investigate exact methods for inverting input tokens from gradient information.
  3. **Efficient Audio Signal Processing.** The final theme focuses on optimizing audio signal processing. We develop computationally efficient architectures that reduce algorithmic latency for high-fidelity speech enhancement, enabling real-time deployment on resource-constrained devices and apply generative models for echo cancellation.

Thesis Committee: Peter Chin (chair), Bryce L. Ferguson, Soroush Vosoughi, and Trac D. Tran (Johns Hopkins University)

12 pm - 1 pm DCC Grand Rounds with Alexi Tulin, PhD DHMC, Auditorium E

Dr. Alexei Tulin earned his Ph.D. from Moscow State University in 1998.  From 1999 to 2004, he completed postdoctoral training in the laboratory of Dr. Allan Spradling at the Carnegie Institution of Washington.  In 2004, Dr. Tulin joined the faculty at Fox Chase Cancer Center, where he was promoted to Associate Professor with tenure in 2010.  In 2017, he relocated his research team to the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the University of North Dakota (UND) School of Medicine & Health Sciences.  He is currently a Professor in the Epigenetics Program at UND. 

Dr. Tulin is internationally recognized for discovering a fundamental role of Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase 1 (PARP1) in chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation.  His research demonstrated that PARP1 regulates gene expression by synthesizing poly(ADP-ribose) (pADPr) polymers on chromatin-associated proteins, leading to localized chromatin relaxation and transcriptional activation at specific genomic loci.  His laboratory’s research program spans four major areas of PARP1 biology:  1) the molecular mechanisms governing PARP1 recruitment and enzymatic regulation; 2) the role of PARP1 in chromatin remodeling, epigenetic bookmarking, and identification of its genomic targets; 3) regulation of the pADPr pathway by Poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase (PARG); and 4) translational and clinical applications of PARP1 modulation.

His laboratory has initiated a translational research program focused on exploiting PARP1 as a therapeutic target in cancer.  Building on his foundational discoveries, his team is developing highly selective PARP1 inhibitors that specifically target histone-mediated mechanisms of PARP1 activation, with the goal of achieving improved precision and efficacy in cancer treatment.

Dr. Tulin’s research has been continuously supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Department of Defense (DoD), the National Science Foundation (NSF), and several private foundations.

2 pm - 3 pm PhD Thesis Proposal: Ya Tang academic Rm B45, ECSC/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Thermoelectric generators and catalysts provide two important pathways for sustainable energy conversion through waste heat recovery and chemical conversion, respectively. However, most existing studies focus primarily on improving material-level performance and provide limited manufacturing guidance for enhancing structural-level properties and system-level functionality. This thesis investigates the design and manufacturing of structured thermoelectric and catalytic materials with a focus on tailoring structural features to enhance their energy-conversion performance.  

The first part focuses on improving output voltage and power of existing Bi2Te3-based thermoelectric materials by optimizing their structural architecture and manufacturing processes. Metastructure design is carried out computationally to balance heat dissipation and electrical resistance. Compared to the traditional bulk TE leg design, the optimized 2D metastructure can double the output power with good mechanical strength. At the system level, metastructure heat sinks and turbulators are integrated with water cooling to further improve thermoelectric performance. The second part extends structural design and 3D printing to catalytic materials. Direct Ink Writing is used to fabricate open-cell zeolite catalysts with up to 90.5 wt.% zeolite loading. Catalyst architecture and Co/Mo doping are further optimized to reduce pressure drop and improve mechanical strength by 4.39-fold over the state of the art.

To further improve power and mechanical strength, a meta-composite TE leg is proposed by combining a dense Bi-Sb-Te core, manufactured via liquid-phase sintering, with a 3D-printed alumina shell-fin structure. The effects of heat dissipation, TE core fabrication, and structural design on thermoelectric and mechanical performance will be systematically evaluated. In addition, the energy recovered by TE materials can be used to accelerate catalytic chemical conversion. An integrated TE-catalyst system that combines thermoelectric energy harvesting with catalytic electrolysis is proposed for hydrogen generation. The electrical power generated by the TE will directly drive the electrolysis reaction, thereby eliminating the need for an external power source.

Thesis Committee: Yan Li (Chair), Jifeng Liu, Will Scheideler, Xianhui Zhao (ORNL)

6:30pm A Walk Back in Time: The Secrets of Cellar Holes Smyth Public Library 55 High Street Candia NH 03034

Northern New England is full of reminders of past lives: stone walls, old foundations, a century-old lilac struggling to survive as the forest reclaims a once-sunny dooryard. What forces shaped settlement, and later abandonment, of these places? Adair Mulligan explores the rich story to be discovered in what remains behind. See how one town has set out to create an inventory of its cellar holes, piecing together the clues in the landscape. Such a project can help landowners know what to do if they have archaeological sites on their land and help stimulate interest in a town's future through its past.

7:00pm The Hidden History of Lake Winnipesaukee Merrimack Historical Society 10 Depot St. Merrimack NH 03054

Thought you knew all there was to know about the "Big Lake"? Think again! Lake Winnipesaukee's history goes well beyond the boating and other recreational-related activities we think of today. Join Glenn as he reveals the many facets of this history, including the real story about “America’s Oldest Summer Resort” in Wolfeboro, the religious sect on Gilford’s Governors Island who thought the world was ending, Massachusetts’ early efforts to claim New Hampshire territory as their own, the site of the country’s first college sports rivalry in Center Harbor, the African American community that once existed in Gilmanton, and the only airport of its kind in the entire country in Alton.  Whether you live in the area, are a visitor from elsewhere in the Granite State, or are a summer resident or tourist, these fascinating and enlightening bits of history will change forever how you view New Hampshire’s "Big Lake."

PATHOLOGY AND LABORATORY MEDICINE GRAND ROUNDS- Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center

“To Lump or To Split? Emerging Entities in Soft Tissue Pathology”

David J Papke, MD, PhD

Associated Pathologist, Brigham and Women’s Hospital

Assistant Professor, Harvard Medical School

 

Series Learning Objective: At the conclusion of this learning activity, participants will be able discuss new innovations in the field of pathology including general pathology, laboratory medicine, molecular pathology and/or other advanced biomedical technologies.

 

Target Audience:  Dept. Faculty, Residents, Fellows, and Medical Students.

 

Bio

Dr. David Papke is a pathologist at Brigham and Women's Hospital and Assistant Professor of Pathology at Harvard Medical School. He practices and conducts research in the fields of bone and soft tissue pathology and gastrointestinal pathology, and he has coauthored chapters for the 6th editions of the World Health Organization (WHO) Classifications of Tumors of Soft Tissue and Bone and Tumors of the Digestive System. He serves on the editorial boards of the American Journal of Surgical Pathology, Virchows Archive, Histopathology, Annals of Diagnostic Pathology, the International Journal of Surgical Pathology, and Applied Immunohistochemistry & Molecular Morphology. Dr. Papke's research studies have focused on improving the classification of rare tumors, furthering our understanding of the genetics of neoplasms, and developing biomarkers to improve diagnostic practice. He is passionate about teaching trainees and practicing pathologists, work for which he was award the Pier F. Paci Memorial Award for Excellence in Teaching.

 

Accreditation:

In support of improving patient care, Dartmouth Health is jointly accredited by the Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME), the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (ACPE), and the American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC), to provide continuing education for the healthcare team.

 

American Medical Association (AMA)

5:30pm What the Declaration of Independence Offers U.S. Social Movements Peterborough Town Library 2 Concord Street Peterborough NH 03458

The Declaration of Independence acknowledges a most volatile right: the people's right to rebel. If the people are not happy with their government, then it is within their unalienable rights to "alter and abolish it." In 1776, that right was exercised through armed rebellion. But is that the only way to exercise that right?

In 1963, John Lewis envisioned a different sort of revolution, one that would achieve the ends of freedom and liberty through non-violent means. In this "unfinished revolution," he argued, current enemies are seen as future friends. We'll consider how the language of the Declaration guides social movements, across the political spectrum, to institute a government that seems most likely to protect each other's unalienable rights.

No registration required. Open to all. Building is accessible.

7:00pm Brewing in New Hampshire: An Informal History of Beer in the Granite State Florence H. Speare Museum 5 Abbott Street Nashua NH 03064

Glenn Knoblock explores the fascinating history of New Hampshire's beer and ale brewing industry from Colonial days, when it was home- and tavern-based, to today's modern breweries and brew pubs. Unusual and rare photos and advertisements document this changing industry and the state's earliest brewers, including the renowned Frank Jones. A number of lesser-known brewers and breweries that operated in the state are also discussed, including the only brewery owned and operated by a woman before the modern era. Illustrations present evidence of society's changing attitudes towards beer and alcohol consumption over the years. Whether you're a beer connoisseur or a "tea-totaler", this lecture will be enjoyed by adults of all ages.

6:00pm A Century of Industrial Progress in Berlin Hybrid White Mountains Community College - Fortier Library 2020 Riverside Drive Berlin NH 03570

A Century of Industrial Progress in Berlin will cover some of the interesting and/or more important developments to come from the Brown Company Research Department, and how some of them changed the way Brown Company made pulp and paper. Also discussed will be some of the highlights of how Brown Company and successors used technology to improve the environment.

Ray Danforth is a resident of Shelburne NH and a retired environmental professional with a distinguished career in the paper industry.

This is a hybrid event, and you are invited to attend either in-person or online. To participate online, please email Diane Pelchat at info@berlinnhhistoricalsociety.org.

Thursday, December 3, 2026

6:00pm Songs of Old New Hampshire Oscar Foss Memorial Library 111 south barnstead road Barnstead NH 03225

Drawing heavily on the repertoire of traditional singer Lena Bourne Fish (1873-1945) of Jaffrey and Temple, NH, Jeff Warner offers the songs and stories that, in the words of Carl Sandburg, tell us "where we came from and what brought us along." These ballads, love songs and comic pieces, reveal the experiences and emotions of daily life in the days before movies, sound recordings and, for some, books. Songs from the lumber camps, the decks of sailing ships, the textile mills, and the war between the sexes offer views of pre-industrial New England and a chance to hear living artifacts from the 18th and 19th centuries.

7:00 pm KALOS in Concert Chosen Vale Performance Center, Enfield

$25 – $75

KALOS in Concert

Friday, December 4, 2026

7:00 – 9:00 pm

Chosen Vale Performance Center

KALOS brings together three musicians of remarkable caliber. Ryan McKasson—who made history as the youngest winner of the US National Scottish Fiddle Championship in 1996—handles violin and viola; Eric McDonald—a much-in-demand session musician—provides guitar and mandolin. McLane, whose musical journey spans classical piano, blues, Indonesian gamelan, and West African drumming, rounds out the trio on accordion and piano. Each player can all croon like there’s no tomorrow.

The trio spans three generations, three cities and two countries. Ryan McKasson (violin, viola, voice), Eric McDonald (guitar, mandolin, voice) and Jeremiah McLane (accordion, piano, voice) met over the years at highland games, contra dances and fiddle camps across North America. They made their first recording in 2016 and have been touring together since 2019. Kalos prizes the magic of live performance—breathing, dancing and weaving together like high-wire acrobats. They are as generous as they are virtuosic. Like nature itself, their music is full of chaos and chance yet always feels spacious and balanced. Their concerts are more an exposé than a performance—they are immersive, trance-inducing experiences.

11:00am Discovering New England Stone Walls Fiske Free Library 108 Broad St. Claremont NH 03743

Why are we so fascinated with stone walls? Kevin Gardner, author of The Granite Kiss, explains how and why New England came to acquire its thousands of miles of stone walls, the ways that they and other dry stone structures were built, how their styles emerged and changed over time, and their significance to the famous New England landscape. Along the way, Kevin occupies himself building a miniature wall or walls on a tabletop, using tiny stones from a five-gallon bucket.

$70 – $75

Holiday Balsam Wreath Workshop

December 7th, 4:30 – 6:30 pm, Great Stone Dwelling

Instructor: Marya Merriam of Wood Frog Flowers

Welcome the winter season with a hands-on wreath-making workshop led by Marya Merriam of Wood Frog Flowers. Participants will learn to create a beautiful 16-inch balsam wreath using fragrant, locally sourced balsam and an assortment of natural materials, including birch bark, red dogwood branches, milkweed pods, cedar, and pinecones.

Whether you’re an experienced crafter or trying wreath-making for the first time, this workshop offers an opportunity to explore natural materials and create a unique seasonal decoration to enjoy at home or give as a thoughtful holiday gift. Participants will leave with a handmade wreath that celebrates the beauty and fragrance of the winter landscape.

About the Instructor

Marya Merriam is the founder of Wood Frog Flowers, a flower farm based on the organic vegetable farm in Vermont where she grew up. With a lifelong connection to farming, Marya began growing and drying flowers while working full-time on a dairy farm. Since 2020, Wood Frog Flowers has grown from a weekend hobby into a full-season venture offering dried flower arrangements, holiday balsam wreaths, and hands-on workshops. Marya’s work celebrates the creativity of seasonal flowers and locally foraged materials while reflecting her commitment to sustainable farming and community.

Workshop Details

Instructor: Marya Merriam of Wood Frog Flowers

All day Motivational Interviewing 2-Day workshop Berry Library, LINK classroom

All dates: Dec 8, Dec 11

Winterim 2026 Motivational Interviewing Training—Register by December 1 here: https://forms.gle/MUtMqUie1dGKRXzH8

Dartmouth Dialogues: Motivational Interviewing Two-Day Workshop

Tuesday, December 8 and Friday, December 11*
9 a.m.–4:30 p.m. (morning refreshments available at 8:30 a.m.)

Location: Berry 180A; the LINK classroom. First Floor Berry Library.

The Student Wellness Center, with support from Dartmouth Dialogues, offers this intensive, interactive (and fun!) two-day workshop aimed at building basic proficiency in Motivational Interviewing (MI). MI is a collaborative communication style for supporting individuals through growth and change.

MI trainings are named in Dartmouth's Commitment to Care strategic plan as “effective skill-building trainings that support high-quality mentoring, advising, and teaching.” 

This evidence-based approach has broad application for working with students (and others) and can be an instrumental tool for advisors, coaches, facilitators, and educators. The training is free and open to the entire Dartmouth community. Morning refreshments, snacks, and lunch will be provided.

Facilitated by Caitlin Barthelmes, member of the MI Network of Trainers and LB White of the Student Wellness Center. 

 *Please attend both days. We offer this training twice a year. If you can't commit to the full training this time, please plan to attend the event when it is offered next summer.

Dec 8 Dec 9 Dec 10
12 pm - 1 pm DCC Grand Rounds with Richard J. Barth, Jr. MD DHMC, Auditorium E

Richard Barth studied Biochemistry and rugby at Princeton, graduated from Harvard Medical School, did his general surgery training at the New England Deaconess Hospital and a surgical oncology fellowship at the National Cancer Institute.

A member of the Dartmouth Geisel School of Medicine faculty for the last 33 years, Dr. Barth is a busy cancer surgeon, operating on over 300 patients annually. He was awarded the 2021 Leonard Tow Humanism in Medicine Award by the Dartmouth faculty for exemplary compassion, empathy and respect for patients and for excellence in the art of medicine.

A Professor of Surgery, Dr. Barth is author of over 120 papers. His research efforts initially focused on immunotherapy, translating findings in mouse models into clinical trials of a dendritic cell vaccine in colorectal cancer patients. In subsequent research he was one of the first to identify that opioids were being overprescribed after surgery and then established guidelines for appropriate opioid prescribing after inpatient and outpatient surgery. For the past decade he has been collaborating with Thayer School engineers to develop a new device and guidance system to improve the accuracy of lumpectomy for breast cancer. Together they founded a company, CairnSurgical, Inc, to manufacture this device and have tested this guidance system in clinical trials.

Thursday, December 10, 2026

10:00am New Hampshire's One-Room Rural Schools: The Romance and the Reality Marion Gerrish Community Center 39 West Broadway Derry NH 03038

Hundreds of one-room schools dotted the landscape of New Hampshire a century ago and were the backbone of primary education for generations of children. Revered in literature and lore, they actually were beset with problems, some of which are little changed today. The greatest issue was financing the local school and the vast differences between taxing districts in ability to support education. Other concerns included teacher preparation and quality, curriculum, discipline, student achievement and community involvement in the educational process. Steve Taylor explores the lasting legacies of the one-room school and how they echo today. 

"The speaker was just terrific. The material was coming out freely and not like a lecture or just reading off of a page of notes. His anecdotes were great and he was entertaining and funny. The hour flew by. I could have listened to him even longer."

-HTG program participant

Our Center is conveniently located in dowtown Derry with amply parking in our lot and on the street. We are completely handicap accessible with an exterior, side entrance ramp, and elevator inside and an accessible restroom on the first floor. Coffee & refreshments with be served.

Julie Taymor's (Broadway's 'The Lion King') astonishing English-language production of Mozart's enchanting fairy tale has become a beloved tradition for family audiences.

The Met made history in December 2006 when it presented its first Live in HD transmission to cinemas worldwide: Julie Taymor's adaptation of Mozart's The Magic Flute. An abridged, English-language production conceived by the Tony Award-winning director of Broadway's The Lion King, this opera returns to select movie theaters for a special encore presentation during the holiday season. Taymor's whimsical production features a winning ensemble, including tenor Matthew Polenzani, baritone Nathan Gunn and bass René Pape. With dazzling puppets and a colorful setting, Mozart's enchanting musical fairy tale is one of the ultimate seasonal sensations for family audiences.

Moravian Star Christmas Ornament Workshop

Join artist and instructor Mary Ann Haagen for a hands-on workshop creating beautiful Moravian star Christmas ornaments! Learn the traditional paper-folding and weaving technique used to make these intricate, multi-pointed stars, which have long been associated with the Advent and Christmas seasons.

Made from four identical paper strips, these three-dimensional stars are a festive way to add handmade charm to your holiday decorations. Create ornaments to hang on your Christmas tree, give as thoughtful gifts, or display throughout your home.About the Instructor

Mary Ann Haagen is a longtime independent Shaker scholar, retired music teacher, and visiting scholar in the Music Department at Dartmouth College. Her research focuses on the Enfield, New Hampshire, Shaker community, and she has been actively involved with the Enfield Shaker Museum since 1987. She is also the founding director of the Enfield Shaker Singers and lectures widely on Shaker history, music, and dance.

Dr. Janielle P. Maynard is an Assistant Professor of Pathology and Oncology at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Her research interests involve the investigation of immunobiological factors that contribute to disease aggressiveness and cancer health disparities. Her work uses molecular pathology, transcriptomic, and translational approaches to characterize the inflammatory landscape of cancer tissues aimed at defining the biology of inflammation-mediated carcinogenesis and testing the efficacy of targeting P2 purinergic receptors for the treatment of aggressive cancers.  

Dr. Maynard graduated with a B.S. from Howard University and earned a Ph.D. in Translational Biology and Molecular Medicine from Baylor College of Medicine. She completed a postdoctoral fellowship in the Department of Pathology at Johns Hopkins where she served as Chief Postdoctoral Fellow in the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center. Dr. Maynard also serves as a co-Director of the Johns Hopkins Postbaccalaureate Research Experience Program (PREP). She is committed to mentoring, and as the founding director of the HBCU Mentoring Program, promotes career awareness and a heightened sense of belonging in the biomedical sciences community. Dr Maynard was awarded the Johns Hopkins Medicine Inaugural Postdoctoral Excellence in Mentoring Award and the Institute for Excellence in Education’s (IEE) Education Award in Mentorship, Advising and Coaching.

6:30pm Historic Lighthouses and Keepers of New Hampshire & Southern Maine Smyth Public Library 55 High Street Candia NH 03034

Jeremy D'Entremont highlights the fascinating stories of the lighthouse keepers and their families who, beginning in 1771, mainainted the lighthouses between Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and York, Maine: Portsmouth Harbor Light, Whaleback Light, White Island (Isles of Shoals) Light, Boon Island Light, and Cape Neddick "Nubble" Light. The histories of these lighthouses and their keepers reveal rich human interest stories and fascinating lore, from rescues and heroism to isolation and tragedy, and even ghost stories. The program also explores ongoing efforts to preserve these iconic maritime sentinels today.

Saturday, January 9, 2027

10:03am Beginner’s Mind for Writing: How to Start Anything through Mindful Writing Dublin Public Library 1114 Main Street Dublin NH 03444

Do you have something in you that wants to be written? It doesn’t matter what kind of writing—poem, novel, memoir, speech, newspaper article, or workplace document—you feel a tug to express. For many of us, beginning a new piece of writing can be daunting. How to bring this inchoate sensation to form and structure? We often waste time psyching ourselves up or fantasizing about the perfect final draft. This presentation helps you enter the present moment and begin writing that piece, maybe one you’ve been contemplating for years, within minutes. Every moment is perfect for writing: starting means entering an ongoing river of language. Among several techniques, we’ll practice moment tracking to jumpstart that dream project and embrace where it takes us. This presentation focuses on prewriting and invention, the earliest phases of writing, and welcomes verbal emptiness to develop equanimity.
